articles.title: Ikea’s Xbox collection includes a giant thumbstick stool
articles.summary: Ikea has teamed up with Microsoft to launch a new assortment of Xbox-inspired furniture and home accessories.
articles.body: Ikea has teamed up with Microsoft to launch a new assortment of gaming-inspired furniture and home accessories, coinciding with the 25th anniversary of the first Xbox console. The nine-piece Yxstaby collection (good luck pronouncing that) includes a TV stand, laptop stand, side table, lounge chair, and multi-functional toolbox, with standout products like a stool, cushion, decorative platter, and mirrored display box being specifically designed around recognizable Xbox controller motifs. The Yxstaby range makes it easier to “bring play into a room and tuck everything away afterwards,” according to Ikea’s press release, with each piece created as a collaboration between Xbox and Ikea designers to naturally co-exist alongside the furniture you already own. It makes use of familiar Scandi-themes like neutral colors and shapes, paired with flashes of Xbox’s iconic green that draw attention to the pockets and compartments designed to hold gaming gear. “How people play at home has shifted, and it is as much about relaxing and connecting with others as it is about performing, which changes what the space has to do,” said Ikea product design developer, Philip Dilé. “Together, we set out to make furniture people really want in their home, not furniture they accept because it is what you need to game.” [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The green X-shaped scatter cushion and thumbstick-inspired stool are among the most Xbox-coded pieces in the Yxstaby collection. Ikea says the stool was developed using original 3D design files for the Xbox controller, with the grippy textured surface now serving to prevent your butt from slipping around instead of sweaty thumbs. The lounge chair comes with a mesh pocket on the underside that’s designed to store your game controllers, but it also looks roomy enough for wider items like magazines and large books. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The TV stand is an easel-style design that’s available in white or black (presumably as a nod to the Xbox console color schemes), and features shelves and hooks for holding your various gadgets and gaming accessories. It also comes with castors so it can be wheeled around the home, as does the side table, which includes a green tray for additional storage. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The mirrored display box comes in black or white, and looks ideal for anyone who wants to turn a collection of Xbox gaming controllers into wall decor. The metalic trinket dish is inspired by the D-pad controller, but subtle enough to not appear obviously gaming related. There’s also a wooden toolbox, which is one of the least Xbox-coded looking items in the collection, but Ikea says it also doubles as a laptop stand for some reason. “I queued all night 25 years ago to get my hands on the first Xbox console, so those shapes are nostalgic to me,” says Ikea designer David Wahl. “The challenge was making it work as a stool, with the right seating curve and stability, while still feeling like a thumbstick. It even moves the way a thumbstick does, so it tilts with you while you play.”  Yxstaby will be available online and in Ikea stores sometime this Autumn, although prices and launch dates will vary by market.

articles.title: Fable: After Watching a Full Quest, I Couldn’t Be More Excited to Play It | gamescom 2026
articles.summary: Beer, swearing, and aggressive strangers. I feel at home. After watching a full quest from Fable, I couldn't be more excited to play it. Our preview:
articles.body:
Beer, swearing, and aggressive strangers. Just your average Thursday night in a North London pub. Turns out fantasy isn’t too far from reality, though, with a stroll around Fable delivering the exact same ingredients for an eventful afternoon. A hands-off presentation at gamescom 2026 gave me new insight into developer Playground Games’ Albion and the stories taking place in it. Here, I’ll walk you through everything that was shown, ahead of me going hands-on with Fable and its combat systems later — stay tuned for my impressions of that very soon. For now, it’s time to take a trip through Bowerstone and see what a full quest brings with it.

For those uninitiated in the original Fable trilogy, Bowerstone is the capital of the fantasy world of Albion, and it’s never looked better than it does here. At the beginning of my roughly 15-minute live gameplay demo, our hero, a young woman with a sword on her back, rode up to the portcullis of the looming city. What could be an intimidating sight quickly turned into one of awe, though, with its central keep towering over crooked, smaller buildings that stack up towards it. There’s a pleasing off-kilterness to the town, reflecting the imbalance in its world as good struggles to outweigh evil. The askew rooftops and twisty brickwork marry beautifully with the winding nature of the city’s streets and the uneven cobblestones that make them. It all makes this world feel entirely handcrafted and believably constructed by the people that live there, rather than a dull geometric pattern laid down by an unimaginative city planner.

It’s not just a sight to behold, though, but a city full of purpose. Over 30 businesses are dotted across it, from hairdressers to clothes shops to tattoo parlours. Playground really wants you to create a character entirely in your own image, and make them feel as married to the world you walk them through as possible. Speaking of marriage, our first stop in Bowerstone takes us to the hero’s family home — a cosy, well-kept cottage warmed by a roaring fireplace. Waiting for us are our daughter, Daisy, and spouse, Elliott. The love between him and our hero is still strong, it seems – as she walks away from him, he can’t help but remark, “Ooph, so glad I married all of that”. Steady on, Elliott, we’ve got a village to save.

Briar Hill is that village, and the crux of Fable’s main story. A mysterious red-cloaked figure called Isabel has turned the people of our hometown to stone, and it's up to us to reanimate them. This quest we’re on now seems fairly early on in the plot, and has taken us to the capital to gain access to the Heroes Guild. A previous mission has popped the key to the Guild’s headquarters in our inventory, and so we stroll up to the huge doors with ease. Again, both the exterior and interior architecture and art design on show are wonderful, with a delightful mix of grandeur and deliberate rough edges on show.

Sitting inside the guild is Humphry the Golden, a legendary figure in Albion folklore who appears to have seen better days. Played by Peep Show’s Super Hans supremo, Matt King, he cuts the figure of a bedraggled alcoholic, slumped in a large chair in the darkness. Never meet your heroes has never proved a truer phrase. Proving my point, in a stupor, he asks for a large beer, and we’re presented with our first choice — Playground promises Fable is packed full of both big and small decisions that will impact everything from minor character relationships to major story moments. Do you give Humphry the tankard full of hoppy goodness, or throw it over him in an attempt to wake him up? The latter is chosen, and a pop-up appears on the left of the screen letting us know that he now thinks we’re an arsehole.

Nonetheless, Humphry needs our help. In debt and on the cusp of being evicted, in order to gain his guidance, we’ll need to dig him out of a hole. It turns out that this once-respected hero gambled away the ownership rights of the guild and lost them to Slick Ronnie, a local Bowerstone gang leader. So, it’s now our job to get them back. It doesn’t take us long to get in trouble with this gang, either. One step back onto the streets and we’re faced with a trio of Ronnie’s lackeys who are bothering Billie, described by Playground as a “part-time playwright, full-time orphan.” Dialogue options are given, and an attempt to defuse the situation is made. Unfortunately, for them, violence is deemed necessary.

It’s the first opportunity for us to get a proper look at Fable’s combat, and I’m impressed. It’s always difficult to know how good a game’s action is until you get your hands on it yourself — something I’ll be doing in mere hours — but it certainly looks slick. Sweeping sword slashes are executed. A bow and arrow is fired satisfyingly with a ping into someone's head. A long electric whip is conjured and sent crashing down onto the group. A fireball is sculpted from our hero’s palms and sent blazing into a chest containing a now-unbeating heart. The flexibility on show is great to see, and it appears this won’t be an RPG that restricts your combat options depending on a strict class structure

That encounter earns us a skill point, and a fairly extensive skill tree is flashed up on screen and then closed before I have time to study it in any depth. However, I did see what the skill point was spent on: magical blades, a spell any Fable veteran will no doubt fondly remember. We’ll see in action shortly.

First, it’s time to head to a more down-on-its-luck part of town where Slick Ronnie’s hideout can be found. Of course, the trail takes us to a pub. The Poor House is Ronnie’s chosen watering hole, and after talking to its clientele, it becomes apparent we need access to the back area of the establishment. There are multiple ways in, but we choose the easy road and pay for entry to save time.

Once through the door, we find ourselves faced with another lock we don’t have the key for. This door is unguarded, however, so we put our trusty lockpicking skills to the test and gain swift entry. There’s no Fallout-esque tumbler-rotating minigame to play here, just a simple hold of a button instead. Ronnie’s office waits on the other side, and the deeds to the guild are there to be plundered. Just walking away would be far too simple, though, wouldn’t it? On the way out, Ronnie isn’t very happy to see us, and a quick attempt to bluff her by saying we wandered into this restricted area after a few too many drinks doesn’t go down well. It’s time to fight again, and the perfect opportunity for those magical blades to see some action.

Upon triggering the attack, three glowing blue swords float above our heads before darting towards an enemy each – it’s very much the spell you remember, and a good indicator that Playground has no intention of abandoning Fable’s history. It appears to be a great crowd control tool when surrounded by multiple attackers, as we are here. A follow-up arrow to one of their knees makes one satisfyingly stumble as they react to the target damage, and then met with the pointed end of our sword. Things then get a little trickier here, as a bulky brute wielding a two-handed axe enters the fight. It’s instantly noticeable how many more hits he can take, so instead it seems wise to focus on building up his stagger bar through sustained attacks so a big damage window opens. Again, I’m impressed by the fluidity of the action.

This battle signals the end of our time with Fable for now, but it's that combat that I can’t wait to get my hands on. I’m left convinced by the enjoyably British tone of the world, the range of characters that inhabit it, and the stories they’re eager to tell us. I’m left hopeful the combat matches that quality, though, and will be finding out very soon if Fable feels as slick to play as it looks. I’ll let you know very soon.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: Mega Man: Dual Override Feels Like a Perfect Entry Point Into The Series
articles.summary: We played Mega Man: Dual Override, which is shaping up to be a perfect entry point into the series.
articles.body:
My earliest video game memories are tied to the Blue Bomber. Barely four years old and playing through Mega Man 2 and 3 on the NES, I somehow made my way through their challenging levels. I won’t say that at that age I could comprehend the precision engineering behind their action-platforming, but I always knew there was something about those games that just felt fantastic. Fast forward 30 years, and I found myself sitting in Capcom’s offices feeling the same sensation. Mega Man: Dual Override understands that it's part of a series built firmly on its tight gameplay foundations, and from my brief time going hands-on with it, it’s looking like a worthy return for Dr Light’s most loyal creation.

As much as things change, they stay the same. Greeting me on the start game screen of Dual Override was the traditional grid of robot masters, all shrouded in mystery for this demo, apart from one: Twinkle Girl. Choosing the order you take on bosses is a key part of any Mega Man strategy, but while that decision was taken away from me for this small slice, another new dilemma was presented in its place. Before entering a stage, you’ll be offered one of three Chip Sets. These are:

Built for Survival: A custom chip that creates a barrier against one instance of enemy fire and grants use of an emergency health-restoring E-Tank.

Built for Fire Power: A custom chip packed with auto-charging that helps you attack more efficiently, plus the power to unleash double charge shots at once.

No Chip Support: For the traditional Mega Man experience, with no added abilities, except for the ability to call in Rush, your jump-pad dog.

Because I’m a stubborn bastard, I chose the latter.

Things didn’t start out too badly — each robot master’s area is made up of three stages, with the first of Twinkle Girl’s not giving me too many problems. A classic mix of precision platforming, dodging enemy projectiles, and firing upon Mets (the hard-hatted enemies who pop up and become vulnerable when you get close) makes up much of the industrial-looking level, and it really felt like reactivating a long-dormant part of my brain. That Mega Buster cannon arm still feels as good as it did decades ago.

Then came Big Press Don. Each stage has its own mini boss, and this giant, red, jet-packed lump of metal was my first real test. Thankfully, I still had a full tank of special ammo available to me, so I hopped into the air to reach Don’s vulnerable head and barraged him with the whole nine yards. I don’t know what other Robot Master this skill is borrowed from — as is Mega Man tradition, you take on the skills of your fallen foes — but it dressed me in a turquoise outfit with an orange-visored helmet alongside a “gun” that propelled me forward in a powerful dash. It’s safe to say Don didn’t like it, as a few hits drained his health bar in seconds. It’s hard to make definitive calls on strategy in a demo as short as this, but I’m guessing this dash weapon was his weakness; after all, finding the most efficient weapons to take on each big enemy, and the order to take them on, has long been the key to solving the overall Mega Man puzzle.

And so onto the second stage I went, and deeper into the giant robot exhibit that Twinkle Girl had decided to call home. I definitely felt the difficulty creep up a little here, with the platforming in particular increasing in complexity. More moving lifts entered the fray as timing jumps became all the more crucial, especially when leaping over firework cannons that would erupt their damaging sparkles in intermittent bursts.

But the biggest surprise came at the end of these few minutes of platforming when I entered the next boss room. Upon being locked in, the tech-filled room shifted into an augmented reality amongst the stars. But that was only the first unexpected thing to happen. That’s because this new space is home to a copy of Astro Man, one of Mega Man 8’s robot masters. This returning foe packs the same moveset as he did on the original PlayStation, complete with swooping lunges, annoying twin spheres that spin around him, and raining green meteors that deal big damage if you mistime your approach. It’s a shinier version of the 30-year-old fight, but I can’t help but feel slightly disappointed that no new attacks or quirks have seemingly been included. It would be nice to see Dual Override referencing the past while remixing it, rather than simply recreating old memories.

On one hand, I enjoyed fighting him again. But on the other, it’s also where my earlier hubris caught up with me. With neither of the more beneficial chip sets selected at the start of my run, I was finding him a real challenge to take down. Rush simply wasn’t going to help me here. And so, knowing my demo time was limited, I finally gave in, restarting the stage with the energy barrier shield equipped. Smart employment of this, plus knowing when to enter the titular Override mode to increase my damage output, soon made quick work of him. Dual Override is also very kind in granting you a checkpoint just outside the boss room, letting you get back into the action within a few seconds of defeat – a “modern” concession that classic Mega Man would never offer.

Peculiarly, I found that second stage to be the toughest part of my demo, with the final section providing less of a challenge. Perhaps this is because it played to my skill set better. I like front-foot, aggressive battles, and that is exactly what my showdown with Twinkle Girl gave me. From first shot to last, our fight lasted less than a minute due to her glass-cannon nature. She’s deadly, but seemed to be more vulnerable to my attacks, especially the aforementioned special weapon. She dashes quickly across the screen, plummets downwards like a furious phoenix, and unleashes starbursts of colourful fireworks. Weave in and out of these deadly displays, and she’s yours for the taking, her weapon yours. Frustratingly, though, I didn't get to see what her armament is called, or get to try it out for myself. I appreciate the variety I’ve already seen in Dual Override’s boss battles, though, and look forward to seeing what else awaits further down the road.

This is the first mainline Mega Man game in almost a decade, so Capcom has had plenty of time to think about what it wants to do with the series. Some things are a constant — precision platforming, tight fights, and the vibrant, animated stages they take place on, soundtracked by toe-tapping electronic tunes — but there’s enough new here to ensure it feels like a Mega Man for the 2020s. It’s too early to see if these new optional chip sets, override mode, and multi-stage Robot Master encounters with increased checkpointing will be an overall positive — but if nothing else, they certainly signal the developer's aim to make this entry more approachable. I remain hopeful, though. There’s still plenty of challenge to be found here, and I had a lot of fun returning to Mega Man with Dual Override. If these tweaks mean a lot more people can set foot in a series that once offered me a gateway into video games, then I’ll be more than happy.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: Marvel Fans Say Avengers: Endgame Encore's Extra 4 Minutes Risk Being 'Really Oversold', After Directors Insist Movie is 'Required Viewing for Following The Story in Doomsday'
articles.summary: We all love Avengers: Endgame, but some Marvel fans are now suggesting that the four minutes of footage added to its upcoming Encore re-release risk being oversold by its directors.
articles.body:
We all love Avengers: Endgame , but some Marvel fans are now suggesting that the four minutes of footage added to its upcoming Encore re-release risk being oversold by its directors.

Endgame is one of the best Marvel movies of all time — perhaps the best — and so it's not surprising to see it return to theaters this fall ahead of Avengers: Doomsday's arrival. Not only will this new chance to watch the film inject a few more million into its box office total (perhaps enough to overtake Avatar once again!), the experience will likely remind cinema audiences of the excitement felt at the close of the Infinity Saga, as a decade of storytelling came to a natural conclusion.

But after the reveal that Avengers: Endgame Encore will be just four minutes longer than the movie's original runtime, fans are revisiting recent comments by directors Joe and Anthony Russo — who suggested that an Endgame watch (or rewatch) was "required viewing" to follow Doomsday's own story — with a healthy dose of scepticism.

From Iron Man to Endgame: How The Avengers' Salaries Changed

A clip of the Russos discussing Avengers: Endgame Encore at San Diego Comic-Con last month is now being shared widely on social media, where the duo discussed why they thought fans should see the film again with Fandango .

"It's going to connect the story of the two movies," Joe Russo said of Avengers: Endgame Encore. "There's a natural progression from Endgame into Doomsday, which is also inclusive of all the other stories that have been playing out.

"But I think it's important to see Endgame in theaters again for two reasons," he continued. "One, if you want to have a lot of fun cheering and screaming and reliving all the emotions you had the first time you saw it. Two, I think it's required viewing for following the story in Doomsday.

"If you saw Endgame when it was originally released, you couldn't see this coming," Anthony Russo added.

Anthony and Joe Russo break down what fans can expect to see in Avengers Endgame: Encore. Tickets are on sale NOW! Assemble your friends, and get your tickets now👇 pic.twitter.com/AaFAk5c1rf — Fandango (@Fandango) August 25, 2026

Anthony and Joe Russo break down what fans can expect to see in Avengers Endgame: Encore. Tickets are on sale NOW! Assemble your friends, and get your tickets now👇 pic.twitter.com/AaFAk5c1rf

Marvel has not detailed what the new footage added to Avengers: Endgame Encore will comprise, though there's a growing sense among fans that it is likely to be scenes shot during Avengers: Doomsday's production that may also end up within Doomsday itself. Many fans believe this is likely to focus on the journey of Steve Rogers — perhaps showing him returning the Infinity Stones, or returning home to Peggy Carter afterwards, only for his peace and quiet to be swiftly disturbed.

In general, though, there's a sense among fans that Marvel would not actually make Avengers: Doomsday incomprehensible without prior MCU knowledge, and certainly not without actually requiring fans to rewatch a movie that released years ago with a few minutes of extras added on. Doomsday will do very well at the box office regardless, of course, but would hardly benefit if its plot hinged on something that only those who attended a screening of Endgame Encore could understand.

"It's literally four extra minutes of footage that will be in a YouTube short within two days," wrote one Marvel fan, in the top comment of a new and lengthy reddit thread discussing the Russo's claims. "I mean I'm probably still gonna go see it just because Endgame was great, and I'd love to see it again in Dolby, but they are really overselling this extra footage, I think."

"Yeah. Not getting a babysitter," a second fan wrote. "Spending $30-$40 for four minutes of footage. A little tone deaf to say 'required viewing'. I'll wait for the leaks."

Marvel Phases 1-3: The MCU's Infinity Saga Ranked

"Normal fans aren't going to go shell out $100 for something they can watch for free on Disney+," wrote another fan. "They are going to be unaware there's a few minutes of additional footage. They'll be there for Doomsday though."

"The last thing this world needs is f***ing DLC for movies," added yet another.

"What do you expect them to say?" countered another fan. "'Skip this one guys, it's only 4 extra minutes and you can just watch a recap video on YouTube.' Like of course they're gonna oversell it lol it's their job."

"Am I gonna go see it? Yes," one fan wrote on X/Twitter. "But are you guys false advertising infinity vision and just trying to make more money because it's only [four] minutes, absolutely."

Marvel has currently made no suggestion it will detail exactly what its new Encore footage will contain, likely meaning audiences will find out for themselves when the film's re-release rolls around next month. Will you be going as well? Avengers: Endgame Encore arrives in theaters on September 25 ( with Iron Man and Infinity Gauntlet popcorn buckets ) before Avengers: Doomsday finally lands on December 18.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Rockstar Games Finally Addresses Extraordinary and 'Heartbreaking' GTA 6 Leaks, Warns Players That 'Some Spoilers' May Now Impact 'The Intended Game Experience'
articles.summary: Rockstar Games has finally addressed the past week's extraordinary spate of Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks.
articles.body:
Rockstar Games has finally addressed the past week's extraordinary spate of Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks, describing the situation as "heartbreaking" for its development team and "unfortunate" for fans.

In a statement posted to social media, the developer acknowledged that its intended experience for players "may now be impacted by some spoilers", but reiterated GTA 6's previously-confirmed launch date of November 19.

The past week has seen more than a dozen gameplay clips appear online , posted by an individual or group that has claimed to be leaking material to highlight the death of physical media and the impact this will have on game ownership, while also charging fans to vote on further leaks using cryptocurrency, in what is widely-seen as a money-making exercise .

Today's statement by Rockstar makes no mention of its efforts to try and stop these leaks from occuring , or the legal processes it has begun to try and determine the identity of the leaker(s) . Indeed, the statement could be read as an admission that the leaks will likely continue — and worsen, with story spoilers likely — at least in the short term.

As if to confirm this, a 15th clip of GTA 6 has just been posted online, within minutes of Rockstar's statement being made public. It show the leaker driving at night, and then a clip of a cutscene with GTA 6 co-protagonist Lucia. This is particularly noteworthy as the leaker has, so far, only shown off gameplay with the character of Jason, though has suggested that a Lucia story prologue could be leaked in future. Watermarked text includes: "Show support trade $Cyberleek," in reference to the leaker's virtual currency, and "let's get 50m trading volume."

"We know that many of you have been waiting to hear from us regarding the events of the past week," Rockstar Games wrote. "It would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto 6 gameplay leak in this way has been heartbreaking for our team, and this is obviously not how we intednd for you to see the game after all this time.

"We are very sorry that everything has taken as long as it has — from getting the game finished (nearly there!) to sharing more details and official gameplay, and providing the community with everything you want to know.

"We are very excited for everyone to see the Extended Look tomorrow," Rockstar continued. "It has taken longer than we wanted to get it ready, but as with everything we do, we know we need to exceed your expetations, and we are determined to deliver at the level you expect and deserve. While it is unfortunate that the intended game experience may now be impacted by some spoilers, we hope that everyone will wait a bit longer to experience the game for themselves on November 19.

"We want to thank everyone in the community who has reached out with messages of support this past week — your words have meant more to this team than you can imagine. Ultimately, we are making this game for you, and without you, we would not have the privilege of making games. We look forward to sharing more with you soon."

From a Take-Two and Rockstar perspective, significant damage is being done as the leaks continue, with numerous sections of the GTA 6's world now revealed. More worrying still, according to Bloomberg , Rockstar still doesn’t know how these leaks happened, nor who is behind them. And while there are no plans to shift this week’s big Netflix reveal, Bloomberg reported that there is frustration and anger internally at recent events, with management sending morale-boosting emails to staff.

Former Rockstar Games technical director Obbe Vermeij, however, downplayed the damage caused by the leaks . Vermeij, who worked at Rockstar North from 1995 to 2009, took to social media to say the Hot Coffee scandal was much more damaging than these GTA 6 leaks.

Rockstar Games will fully reveal GTA 6 gameplay itself later this week via the Grand Theft Auto 6 Extended Look, a lengthy and official deut that will be released exclusively on Netflix for six hours, before arriving on other platforms such as YouTube. articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Switch 2 Gameplay (Off-Screen) | gamescom 2026 - IGN

articles.title: I Finally Found My Dream Collectible, and It Only Took 40 Years of Searching for It
articles.summary: I spent 40 years looking for a collectible prop replica of the Omni, the time-travelling device from the mostly forgotten show Voyagers!, and now I've finally found one.
articles.body:
Not to date myself, but it was, oh, 40 years ago or so when I first watched the now mostly forgotten TV show Voyagers! as a kid. A time-travel romp with an occasionally steampunk vibe, the short-lived series featured a kid as one half of its time-hopping duo, so the self-identification factor was built into the show for the young’uns like me who were watching. On top of that, the kid (Jeffrey, played by Meeno Peluce) was kind of a nerd – big on history and basically the “smart one” in his pairing with the “Voyager” Phineas Bogg (the late Jon-Erik Hexum). Hey, I knew about the Wright brothers too – maybe I could also be a time-traveller!

But the real appeal of Voyagers! for me was in the time-travel mechanism that the Voyagers like Bogg used: the Omni. For whatever reason, this thing really hit me where I lived.

The Omni was a handheld device that, while sci-fi by its very nature, was very much centered in that steampunk design realm. Seemingly cast in brass and complete with mechanical dials and a tiny globe that allowed its user to zero in on a specific time and place to travel to, the Omni also had rivets and a hinge that its cover hung from, red and green lights, and a push-button mechanism to activate it. The prop’s very design also told a story about the Voyagers (a group of time-travellers whose mission is to make sure the timeline stays on track) that the short-lived show never quite got the chance to do: These people were advanced enough to invent time travel, yet they preferred their tech to be more Jules Verne than Gene Roddenberry in style.

So anyway, I became fixated on this hunk of metal. And you know, this was of course way before the internet, so it wasn’t like you could just google “voyagers omni” to learn more about the device, or the show, or how the prop was made. It also didn’t help that Voyagers! was cancelled after its first season and basically consigned to TV oblivion for decades, so all a kid like me had was my memories of the Omni to keep this particular bit of fandom going. (My fixation on the watch-like Omni was certainly tied to my interest in the even-more-forgotten TV movie The Girl, the Gold Watch & Everything , which was about a gold pocket watch which could stop time. Which is without a doubt why I got a pocket watch as my First Communion gift!)

The thing is, eventually I did google “voyagers omni” and I realized that there were various fans out there who’ve attempted to build their own Omnis over the years. And some of them have looked pretty amazing , too. But they always seemed hard to find and/or very expensive. Still, that changed for me recently when I discovered a (mostly) 3D-printed version of the Omni on Etsy . At like $250, it was a steal, and so I finally got my own. Check it out:

Is it perfect? No. Is it an affordable chance to have a semi-forgotten piece of TV history displayed on my book shelf? Heck yeah, it is. While the prop replica is mostly made of resin, unlike the more expensive version currently available which is brass (and runs over $1000 now), the dials on this piece are actually brass and do in fact rotate. The lid flips open as well, and there’s a belt clip if you plan on cosplaying as Bogg (or Jeffrey). The lights don’t blink and it doesn’t emit any sounds either, but again… for me this is a display piece that falls right in my price range.

But hey, if they ever add an actual time-travel chip to it, maybe I’ll eventually spring for the more expensive version that’s floating around out there. Until then… as Bogg used to say, green light, kid. We did it!

Talk to Scott Collura @scottcollura.bsky.social , or listen to his Star Trek podcast, Transporter Room 3 . Or do both!

articles.title: The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones are good, but don’t stand out
articles.summary: ﻿There’s nothing really wrong with the QuietComfort Headphones 2nd Gen, but there’s nothing exciting about them, either.
articles.body: Bose QuietComfort headphones used to be innovative. Bose’s noise-canceling research is the reason the technology is where it is today, and its headphones set the standard. They were the ubiquitous traveler’s accessory. But over the past few years, it’s felt like Bose has rested on that reputation, as other companies have caught up. Sony and Apple have both surpassed Bose in noise-canceling performance, and even midrange headphones like the $130 Soundcore Space 2 are close for much less money. That means the $359 Bose QuietComfort Headphones 2nd Gen need to stand out in other ways — and I don’t think they do. [Product: Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2 | The second-generation Bose QuietComfort headphones look a lot like the QuietComfort Ultra Gen 2 that Bose launched last fall, but with more plastic instead of metal accents in the headband and joints. In addition to black and white, the QC Headphones come in mauve, a light avocado green, and a two-tone mint color, where the padding is darker than the rest of the headphones. The colors look nice, but headphones companies (including Bose) have been expanding on the reliable black and white options for years now, so colorful options are no longer novel. The new QuietComfort Gen 2 are designed as a step-down model from the $449 Ultra Gen 2, but they’re slightly better in a few ways. I usually find Bose headphones, including the Ultra Gen 2, to be bassy with a peaky high end, which the limited 3-band EQ in the app could never quite compensate for. But the default listening mode on the QC Gen 2 headphones is the best I’ve heard from Bose, and I think most people would be more than happy with the sound (I still prefer the stock sound from any of the Sony XM series). I do find the midrange muted, causing vocals to sound buried or snare hits — like at the beginning of The Cranberries’ “Zombie” — to lose their impact. But unlike on previous Bose headphones, I could fix the problem with the 3-band EQ in the app by boosting the mid to +4. It added more presence and settled in nicely between the bass and upper frequencies. [Image: The power button has moved from the outside ear cup face to the bottom, which is a nice visual improvement. Bose built the QuietComfort line’s long-standing reputation on active noise cancellation. The Gen 2’s is solid, but not as strong as the flagship Ultra Headphones. I actually find that to be a good thing, though. I experience a phenomenon dubbed “eardrum suck” on the QC Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen because of their aggressive noise cancellation. It’s a disconcerting feeling that can feel like a change of pressure in your ears (although there’s no actual pressure change). I didn’t feel it with the QuietComfort Headphones, and while their noise-canceling performance isn’t quite as good as the Ultra’s, and certainly not as good as either the Sony XM6 or Apple AirPods Max 2 (which don’t cause eardrum suck for me, for some reason), it’s more than enough to block out airplane noise or AC units, especially when music is playing. While the headphone jack is now gone, the USB-C connection supports both charging and audio (lossless up to 24-bit/48kHz), like the Ultra Gen 2. Bose also includes both a USB-C-to-USB-C and USB-C-to-3.5mm cable (color-matched to the headphones), so it’s still possible to connect to a 3.5mm source. But there’s no AptX Lossless or LDAC wireless high-res codec support (the Ultra Gen 2 support AptX Lossless, and LDAC is supported on a variety of headphones from Sony and others). The QC Gen 2’s call quality is about the same as the Ultra Gen 2’s, and better than previous Bose headphones, but that’s a low bar. Bose still lags behind every major competitor and is light years behind the tech in Soundcore’s Liberty 5 Pro earbuds (which will likely come to its over-ear headphones soon). They add extra sibilance to my speaking voice and in loud environments compress the sound, which can cause sentences to clip, making me hard to understand. [Image: The QC Headphones fold up nicely and include two color-matched cables. Call quality aside, the Bose sound really good (especially with the midrange tweak), they have solid ANC performance, they’re light and relatively comfortable, and they have some nice color options. But the same can be said about the vast majority of headphones out there. There’s nothing about the Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2 that really stands out, especially for $359. Part of the problem is the price, which puts them in a no-man’s-land. Current-gen flagships like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen, Sony WH-1000XM6, and Apple AirPods Max 2 can be found on sale for $400 or a little more, while slightly older — but still competitive — headphones like the XM5 and Sennheiser Momentum 4 are often $250 or less. That’s not to say the second-gen Bose QC Headphones are bad. Far from it. They’re a strong argument against spending the extra money on the Ultra Gen 2, but unless you want Bose headphones in particular, there’s not a compelling reason to get them. The $400 Sony WH-1000XM6 have better noise canceling, great call quality, and LDAC support, and I slightly prefer their stock sound. They even support Auracast with some phones. Apple’s AirPods Max 2 have a distinctive look and the same deep integration with Apple’s ecosystem as the AirPods Pro, and they can be found for as low as $430. [Image: There aren’t major differences with the second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones — and that’s part of the problem. Give me a redesigned look. Give me high-res wireless support. Hell, give me Auracast. Give me any reason to say “the QuietComfort Headphones are the headphones to get” instead of just another iterative update. They aren’t bad headphones by any means, but Bose used to make the best ANC headphones. Now they’re just another pair that are good enough. Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

articles.title: Rockstar finally responds to ‘heartbreaking’ GTA 6 leaks
articles.summary: The Grand Theft Auto developer releases a statement following a week of repeated leaks.
articles.body: Rockstar Games has released its first official statement following days of sustained leaks of footage from Grand Theft Auto VI, calling the period “heartbreaking for our team.” Not long after Rockstar posted, the source of the leaks posted another video clip of the game, this time showing the Jason character pulling off the series’ trademark move of carjacking a box Chevy-like vehicle with a “Rideout Customs” logo across the back window and trying to evade the police. At the end, the other main character of the game, Lucia, appears briefly in what looks like a cutscene. [Image: “It would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay leak in this way has been heartbreaking for our team, and this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time,” the studio said in its statement published Wednesday morning on social media. “We are very sorry that everything has taken as long as it has — from getting the game finished (nearly there!) to sharing more details and official gameplay, and providing the community with everything you want to know.” Footage from the game has been repeatedly shared in recent days from an apparently playable build of the game. A person or organization calling themself “CyberLeek” has claimed responsibility for the leaks, which have been used in part to promote a cryptocurrency. Publisher Take-Two Interactive has requested to be able to subpoena Microsoft and Discord over the copyright-infringing content in the hope of identifying the source of the leaks. On Thursday evening, fans are getting an “extended look” at the game in a show that will stream exclusively on Netflix at 3PM ET, six hours before it appears on YouTube. The long-awaited game itself will release on November 19th. > Dear all, > We know that many of you have been waiting to hear from us regarding the events of the past week. It would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay leak in this way has been heartbreaking for our team, and this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time. We are very sorry that everything has taken as long as it has - from getting the game finished (nearly there!) to sharing more details and official gameplay, and providing the community with everything you want to know. > We are very excited for everyone to see the extended look tomorrow. It has taken longer than we wanted to get it ready, but as with everything we do, we know we need to exceed your expectations, and we are determined to deliver at the level you expect and deserve. While it is unfortunate that the intended game experience may now be impacted by some spoilers, we hope that everyone will wait a bit longer to experience the game for themselves on November 19. > We want to thank everyone in the community who has reached out with messages of support this past week - your words have meant more to this team than you can imagine. Ultimately, we are making this game for you, and without you, we would not have the privilege of making games. > We look forward to sharing more with you soon. > Sincerely, > Rockstar Games Update, August 26th: Added a note about the latest leak.

articles.title: We’ve Seen The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past in Action, and It’s Looking Like Another Blood & Wine | gamescom 2026
articles.summary: We've seen The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past in action - learn about everything we saw on Geralt's new quest to find his missing bard in a cursed garden of thorns.
articles.body:
Geralt carefully circles the Swarmion, his steps slowly overlapping as he sizes up his foe. The creature could be easily mistaken for any generic fantasy undead or humanoid mutant, were it not for the cloud of hornets that swarm around its torso – a bizarre form of armour by any stretch of the imagination. But our Witcher is as resourceful as ever. He switches his silver sword for a chain, swinging the hooked end round and round as he chooses his target. The creature's legs, or its head? The answer is obvious. The hook sinks into the fleshy neck and pulls taught, wrenching the creature out of the hornet swarm and pulling it directly into the path of Geralt’s blade. Blood plumes from its neck. The head falls with a dull thud.

The silver chain is an important weapon for Geralt of Rivia. Those who have been there from the beginning will remember it from The Witcher’s very first cutscene, back in 2007. Those who have been there from the actual beginning will know it from the short story within The Last Wish collection, from which that cutscene was adapted. The important thing is that it’s part of Geralt’s core Witcher gear – and so it’s only fitting that we finally get to use it in what could well be the last time we get to play as him.

Songs of the Past is The Witcher 3’s unexpected third expansion pack , which will launch next year – 12 years after the base game was originally released, and a year ahead of the series’ in-development fourth game , which passes the protagonist baton to Ciri. And Geralt’s chain-swinging monster battle was just one small section of an hour-long demo I watched at gamescom 2026, during which a member of the CD Projekt Red dev team played through the ‘A Bed of Thorns’ quest, an early chapter that establishes Songs of the Past’s story.

Geralt awakens in Letten, the homeland of his frequent partner-in-heroics, Dandelion. While much of Geralt’s life has been well documented across both Witcher books and games, Dandelion’s history is a little more of an enigma – one that Songs of the Past seems primed to crack. The quest’s opening sees Geralt trek towards a grand hilltop estate, the home where Dandelion grew up not as a bard, but as Julian Alfred Pankratz, Viscount de Lettenhove. It’s not hard to see why he left this life of nobility behind; Geralt endures a painfully tense meal with Dandelion’s incredibly stern grandmother, a woman who would make even the most pampered person want to run away from home. Also present is Lilla, Dandelion’s cousin – a much more agreeable woman and Geralt’s new companion (plus, of course, potential target of affection – although this playthrough ignored any flirtatious dialogue options.)

I hesitate to make a judgement call on Songs of the Past's writing at this early stage, but I'll understand if you've some reservations - rather than purely CD Projekt Red behind the wheel, this expansion is the work of Fool's Theory, a different studio (although one that is made up of many CDPR veterans). Thankfully, what I've seen so far suggests the quality bar has been maintained. Within just a single scene I had a very good idea of who these two women were and how their values complimented or clashed with Geralt's own well-established code.

Not at the table is surely the reason Geralt came here in the first place; his faithful bard is nowhere to be seen. And so begins Geralt and Lilla’s mission to seek out Dandelion and bring him home. But where to start? Well, in dreams: during the night Geralt had visions of blood, thorns, violets, and a well – an image Lilla recognises as The Garden of Thorns. The two meet later that day to head out in search of what should just be a bad story, but is very quickly going to become a horrifying reality.

Letten is a beautiful place, divorced from the woes of The Continent. In that way it’s a little like Blood and Wine’s idyllic Toussaint, and the comparisons don’t stop there: CD Projekt Red says to expect something of a comparable size, so it may well be that Songs of the Past extends as far as 30 or so hours. Geralt explores the old and new sides of the town, and we pass by rows of bushes entwined with wild flowers – there’s a little of Nordic midsummer in its design, blended with English and Polish countryside. It all looks beautiful, helped by the newly-announced remaster, which upgrades The Witcher 3’s technology base with higher-resolution textures and path-tracing lighting. It would be disingenuous to say it makes this decade-old RPG look like a game from the current console generation, but it’s nonetheless a beautiful thing, particularly when it comes to natural environments caught in the final rays of the day’s sun.

But a Witcher’s job rarely stays in pleasant territory. It’s not long before Geralt and Lilla have journeyed beyond the town’s borders and found themselves in more cursed lands. Knotted trees with twisted branches form the edge of an arena in which Geralt does battle with a Thornbloom, a large vine-like plant that can cause fields of large bulbs to grow and subsequently explode. While the remaster and, by extension, Songs of the Past benefit from an upgraded combat system, it’s not obvious in this fight how substantial the change is – this very much looks like Witcher combat as usual. A little later, when the Swarmion and its hornet shield turn up, it becomes clear that the chain does add some extra flair to the proceedings, and I like that in a moment of slow-motion you’re able to target what body part Geralt sinks the hook into before grappling a far-off enemy into melee range. But until I go hands-on with the new system I’m going to assume the changes are subtle tweaks rather than a revolutionary overhaul.

Similarly, CD Projekt Red didn’t dedicate much time to exploring Geralt’s upgraded character progression systems, so it’s as yet unclear just how different things are compared to the original version. What I did see, however, were new skill pages that re-arrange the layouts of the abilities in more of a distinct tree shape, so it may be that there’s been a re-thinking of how you progress Geralt through his RPG upgrades… or at least a re-thinking of how that progression is communicated.

Geralt and Lilla continue to push through the forest and eventually make their way to a tightly-woven wall of thorns, its branches laced with violets and human skulls. At its base lies a dying deer, its blood soaked up by the horrifying structure. This is the gate to the Garden of Thorns. Beyond lies answers to the mystery of our missing Dandelion. In another playthrough, Geralt may well have used his intellect to coax those branches open – CD Projekt Red promises that there are multiple ways to navigate this problem. In the interest of time, though, the developer controlling the demo takes the path of violence, slicing the gate apart. The strike causes the garden to grow vines between Geralt and Lilla, separating them. Perhaps this is the consequence for not seeking out a more careful approach to the situation? Either way, Geralt is forced to fight through Giant Centipedes and those aforementioned Swarmions to find his way back to Lilla… and the well.

The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past screenshots

Yes, the well from Geralt’s dream is real, and defended by the Slumbering Knight, this demo’s boss fight. A noble corpse that’s become half tree, it’s able to strike and defend itself with a huge, bark-shrouded arm. But that’s not the interesting thing: around its neck is a chain finished with a horse pendant. The sigil of Lettenhove. This withered warrior is a member of Dandelion’s own house… or at least was, once upon a time. Thankfully, despite the signs this man once wore flamboyant costuming, there’s no suggestion this is Dandelion himself. The search goes on, and the next location is obvious: down the well. Will there be a devil in this one?

Not quite. But the twisted wooden figure within it, which you saw during the trailer for Songs of the Past shown at Opening Night Live, could well be mistaken for one. Quite what it is remains to be seen, as that’s where the gamescom demo suddenly cuts to black. But, considering its prominence in said trailer, this creature likely lies at the heart of this Dandelion-themed mystery.

This first taste of Songs of the Past doesn’t offer up anything radically new or unexpected. This is more of The Witcher 3, even with its remastered tech base and updated combat and ability systems. But it’s wise not to approach this project with the expectations of “new” Witcher – this is an expansion for a 11 year old game, after all. Save that enthusiasm for The Witcher 4. But still, this is an 11 year old game that has summoned me back numerous times already, and even as its joints get creaky, it’s always incredibly clear why The Witcher 3 is a generational-defining RPG. To be able to revisit it once more to play through a whole new story, meet brand new characters, and explore a rich new setting isn’t something I thought I’d ever get to do, and so in some ways that’s more interesting than a brand new game – perhaps with Songs of the Past, CD Projekt Red and Fool's Theory has found a way to make coming back to a well-loved home feel like the first time all over again.

Matt Purslow is IGN's Executive Editor of Features.

articles.title: Rockstar Games Responds to Grand Theft Auto VI Gameplay Leaks Ahead of Extended Look Trailer
articles.summary: Rockstar Games released a statement Wednesday regarding the recent gameplay leaks for the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI video game.
articles.body:
Rockstar Games released a statement Wednesday regarding the recent gameplay leaks for the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI video game.

In the statement, Rockstar Games noted that while it has been "heartbreaking" for the development team to see gameplay get leaked before it was ready to be shown, everyone involved is still "very excited" about the extended look, which will drop Thursday at 3 p.m. ET on Netflix:

York Responded to Ad on Prostitution Site Before Arrest

IGN's Wesley Yin-Poole reported Tuesday that 14 gameplay videos have been leaked, with the most recent ones featuring a nightclub, beach and video game store.

It has been 13 years since the release of Grand Theft Auto V, making GTA VI one of the most long-awaited video games in history.

Originally slated for a 2025 release, GTA VI was pushed back until May 26, 2026, and then again until Nov. 19, 2026.

The initial Grand Theft Auto VI trailer dropped back in December 2023, followed by a second official trailer in May 2025, offering gamers a glimpse into the next generation of one of the most popular video game franchises of all time:

While the trailers helped whet the appetites of those who have been waiting for a new entry in the Grand Theft Auto series for well over a decade, the long wait time for the game's release left Rockstar susceptible to additional leaks.

Rockstar is close to the finish line now with GTA VI being less than three months away from dropping, and Thursday was meant to be the deepest dive into the game yet.

While certain aspects of Grand Theft Auto VI have been spoiled for some gamers who decided to check out the leaks, the extended look figures to represent the most Rockstar has shown off thus far in an official capacity.

The long wait will finally be over and GTA fans will get to see what the game has to offer firsthand on Nov. 19 when Grand Theft Auto VI officially drops on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles.

articles.summary: Star Wars Zero Company reviewed by Dan Stapleton on PC, also available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.Star Wars Zero Company is an excellent tactical game that does a fantastic job of slathering on the same cinematic look and feel we saw in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi games, incorporating strong characters and a storyline that's refreshingly centered on non-Force users and a non-traditional villain. There's more of an emphasis on cooperation and flexibility, and a tighter focus on smaller maps that encourage a radically different and more aggressive playstyle. articles.title: Star Wars Zero Company Is an Excellent Tactical Game That Does a Fantastic Job of Slathering on the Same Cinematic Feel of the Star Wars Jedi Games
articles.summary: An excellent tactical game with the same cinematic feel as the Star Wars Jedi games.
articles.body:
It makes a lot of sense that Star Wars Zero Company is the result of a collaboration between developers of XCOM 2 (now at Bitreactor) and Star Wars Jedi: Survivor (at Respawn). Those two excellent games couldn't be much more different from each other, but their strengths come together here to create a great-looking, clever tactics game that also tells one of the better Star Wars stories we've seen since Rogue One. Excellent characters, writing, music, and cinematic flair give context and weight to a campaign that centers around a diverse group of mercenaries, with Force powers and lightsabers refreshingly taking a back seat to blasters and thermal detonators. And while its turn-based gameplay is instantly familiar to XCOM veterans like me, its more aggressive playstyle and flexible characters make it far more than a simple Star Wars reskin.

The opening cutscene shows the Republic and Separatist fleets blasting away in orbit as the camera zooms in to Clone Troopers fighting battle droids on the ground, but then veers off to the side to focus on a smaller scuffle. That effectively establishes that this story takes place around the periphery of the Clone Wars rather than on its front lines. Our customizable main character, Hawks, is a former military commander who suffered a defeat and went into business for himself (or herself) with a crew of misfits. (If that sounds familiar, it may be because it's also a perfect description of Malcolm Reynolds from Firefly, and Hawks' voice even takes on a slight space cowboy drawl at times – but that's only fair, given how much Mal owes to Han Solo in the first place.)

Hawks and company immediately come into conflict with a Separatist-aligned cult known as the Infinite Coil led by the enigmatic Fathom, who is bent on spreading a mind-altering plague across the galaxy with creepy bugs. While it's hinted that this disease may be Force-adjacent, it's a welcome change of pace to be up against something at least a bit more original than yet another Sith-like villain. Fortunately, Fathom is largely allowed to remain mysterious during her chilling performance, and her relationship with her henchman son prevents her from becoming a two-dimensional villain. And even though it's not playable, she eventually orchestrates a climactic space battle unlike anything we've seen in Star Wars before.

Your main crewmembers all have compelling stories to follow as well, drawing to mind comparisons to Knights of the Old Republic (even though this isn't that kind of RPG and you only rarely make dialogue decisions). What they lack in novelty, they make up for with strong writing and acting: big blue brawler Kabb fills the obligatory role of the alien who talks funny, Jae is a scion of a mining family driven from her home by Coil, Trick is a medically discharged clone with plenty of brothers to help, Cly is the Mandalorian out for revenge, Tel-Rea is an AWOL padawan investigating Coil, and Luco is a sharpshooter who hates the Republic but hates Fathom more. Each of them has their own chain of story missions to complete that include a decent number of twists and cameos from other Clone Wars-era characters.

The personalities that stand out most to me, though, are non-combatants you interact with only at your base, a docked freighter called The Den. Runa is your personnel manager/bookkeeper, and her Separatist background sets her apart from the rest of the crew, who are more aligned with the Republic. She's also the most consistently funny, thanks to her endearing vanity and high level of sass. Her banter with the young, by-the-book Republic Intelligence officer Bennic is always entertaining while you're choosing missions at the holotable display, and she makes him a more sympathetic character as his loyalties are tested by the events of the war. Special mentions for medical droid M-3VO and Neesh, an oversized Lasat arms dealer, both of whom have some good lines.

The other thing you'll do before heading into combat is run Operations, where you'll spend your limited Intel points to pick which off-screen text adventures to dispatch your team on, unlocking more missions and earning cash and loot prizes. A lot of those do feel like blindly rolling the dice because you're asked to pick which team members to send without any indication of who might be better suited for, say, extracting hostages or hacking into a Separatist facility – so when things go wrong and people get injured it feels like, well, missing a 90% shot. But I always had a few bodies to spare on my roster, so that never tripped me up. And some of these are interesting dilemmas that give you a preview breaking down which of your team will be angry if you, for example, sell someone out to a Hutt for a few extra credits.

After you pick a mission and watch the repetitive, unskippable transit cutscene (which tends to hitch on both PC and PS5 Pro) as your team hyperspace-jumps into action, the tactical combat is easy to pick up if you've played anything in the XCOM vein. But while the fundamentals of controlling your team of four, taking cover, lining up attacks, and crossing your fingers that the RNG gods rule in your favor on a percentage to hit are similar, Zero Company is a vastly different game that encourages you to dive into the fray and push the enemy around. You’ll routinely knock them into each other, off of ledges, into an ally's overwatch zone, or line them up for an area-of-effect attack. (Just remember to always have a backup plan, because you're still going to miss those 90% shots 10% of the time.)

A big part of why I felt encouraged to do that is because, even though permadeath is on by default, your troops are pretty hard to kill. A character has to be downed three times (without being healed between missions) before they're gone for good. There also aren't that many surprise attacks, because the maps are usually pretty small and there's no fog of war, meaning you'll never be ambushed by an enemy you couldn't see. On top of that, there are no lasting consequences for taking damage until someone's downed for the first time and becomes injured, so I felt safe to take troops out of cover and into the open to absorb some punishment if it gave me a clear shot or got me close enough to an extraction zone that I could make it out the next turn. Despite that arrogance, in my first 35-hour playthrough on Normal difficulty, I didn't come close to losing anybody (though I come to this with a few thousand hours of XCOM under my belt, so your mileage may vary).

Another major distinction is that it's easy to chain together actions and give your operators more moves in a turn than their default three action points would normally allow. Advantage points are built up every time you damage an enemy (or use some specific abilities), and then you can spend them on extra abilities from any character, such as Trick's rocket launcher or Hawks' ability to grant an extra action point to a squad member. There are plenty of these, and that gives you a great reason to equip at least some people with blaster pistols: they're lower damage and shorter range than rifles, repeaters, or sniper rifles, but they can fire off three (or more) shots per turn to rack up Advantage quickly.

One of the trickier systems to master is the Backup ability that randomly rotates around your squad every turn. The character who has it can designate a teammate within range to assist them, and on their next attack that teammate will take a followup shot that always hits, even if the first shot misses wildly. It's incredibly valuable to have an opportunity to score guaranteed damage on every turn. But you have to be thoughtful about this because it's easy to waste if your backup guy doesn't actually have line of sight on the enemy, or if you land a critical hit and end up killing your target solo.

As much fun as it is to mow down dozens of hapless battle droids and watch them satisfyingly fall to pieces, Zero Company could have done with a bit more enemy variety. To be fair, there are quite a few types, including Coil soldiers who make you consider who's closest when one of them dies because their allies may absorb some of their power. There are melee guys, sniper guys, and everything in between, but pretty much the only non-humanoids you encounter are the rolling, shielded Droidekas. Those are memorable fights, but after a while everything else starts to blend together a bit even if you do have to adapt your tactics.

Many of the story missions stand out at least, partly because they'll do things like force you to move ahead by blowing up the area behind you or have you hold two locations at once and then extract while enemies constantly spawn in. For some of those you'll do a string of battles in a single location, and Zero Company has a cool trick to tie them together: the camera zooms in to third person and you run from one to the next, controlling Hawks directly until you walk into the combat zone. It gives you a much better sense that you're fighting in a real place than in the side missions where, more often than not, you're dropped directly and jarringly into a battle. I do wish there were more to do from that perspective than walk up to a person or thing and push a button to trigger some dialogue, because the levels you walk through look great.

That said, you'll probably see a fair number of graphical bugs during missions, particularly when enemies are air-dropped in, and the camera can get a bit wonky when it zooms in for what's supposed to be a flashy animation and shows you a close-up of a wall instead. A few times after a slow-motion overwatch reaction shot, I thought I might have to force-quit because everything hung for a good 20 seconds before resuming. But I haven't seen anything that noticeably messed me up – I never once had to reload a mission because I felt something hadn't gone according to plan thanks to a glitch. So it's safe to say that Zero Company is substantially less buggy than XCOM 2 when it first came out (and maybe even today).

Character progression is a little strange in that you're given almost complete freedom to remake most of your team at will. Hawks, for instance, can be changed from a Medic one mission to a Sniper the next, and any of the other six specialities after that. You can respec all his skill points and swap his gun out (in a wonderfully nerdy touch, each of the four weapon types has multiple different looks to pick from with their own sound effects) to further customize how you want them to play. The same goes for a lot of minor recruitable characters – excluding the incredibly handy astromech droids, which are purpose-built for handing out action points to teammates and lobbing grenades and healing items like crazy. That level of flexibility certainly encourages experimentation, even if it does make your choices matter a bit less when it comes to building out your team in the long term.

The only real restrictions are on your main crewmates, who can still be respecced but each have a defining class and a unique ability that give you a reason to keep them alive (on top of being able to complete their story missions). Jae's Last Shot triggers a fantastically helpful execution when an enemy's HP falls below a certain threshold, Kabb's melee attack refunds your action points if it kills the target, Cly has a Mandalorian jetpack that sets people on fire as she lands, Trick can resurrect himself once per mission, etc. Tel-Rea, naturally, has her own unique Jedi skill system.

One thing that can't be redone at will is the bond bonuses. When two teammates care about each other very much, they level up their bond and you get to choose between three randomly selected bonuses that apply to both of them, such as increasing ranged damage by one or going a bit farther on their first move. These are pretty small boosts on their own, but they add up over time and will significantly increase some crucial stats if you're consistent with your choices.

Things get doubly complex when you unlock the ability to give each character a secondary class, which lets you split their skill points between two class trees or concentrate on one. That opens up a whole new layer of opportunity for synergizing abilities, weapon mods, and utility items. I feel like I only scratched the surface of this potential on my first playthrough, and I've already started another on Hard to see how much I'll need to fine-tune my builds to survive.

I'm a few hours into that run, and I can already feel that the replayability of Zero Company is a bit limited relative to XCOM 2 because it's more story-focused and lacks the procedurally generated maps and randomized upgrade unlocks that make that game so dynamic. That's a sky-high bar to meet, though, so I'm not holding that against it – and I definitely missed some missions that can expire before you're able to get to them on my first playthrough, so I expect there will be a fair amount of new things to do this time.

articles.title: Brothers - Official Trailer (Apple TV) - IGN
articles.summary:
Check out the trailer for Brothers, an upcoming comedy series starring and executive produced by Academy Award winner Matthew McConaughey and Academy Award nominee Woody Harrelson, and showrun and executive produced by multi-Emmy Award nominee and Peabody winner Lee Eisenberg. The ensemble cast also includes Natalie Martinez, Brittany Ishibashi, Nolan Almeida, Ella Grace Helton, Noah Carganilla, Highdee Kuan, Oona Yaffe and Holland Taylor. The eight-episode comedy will premiere on Apple TV with the first two episodes on Wednesday, September 23, followed by one new episode every Wednesday through November 4, 2026.  

Brothers follows McConaughey and Harrelson, who play fictionalized versions of themselves, and whose friendship is thrown into chaos when they uncover a decades-old secret: they might actually be brothers. After Woody’s daughter’s engagement falls apart, he loads up the family and heads to Austin for an extended stay at Matthew’s ranch. But what begins as a healing getaway quickly spirals when Matthew’s mother, Ma Mac (played by Holland Taylor), accidentally lets slip a long-buried secret that the two friends might actually be brothers. As Woody turns the ranch upside down in pursuit of the truth, Matthew finds himself juggling an entirely different identity crisis: a potential run for Governor of Texas. The result is a heartfelt, chaotic, and wildly funny story about friendship, family, fame, and the messy line between myth and reality.Brothers is produced for Apple TV by Paramount Television Studios. Eisenberg, McConaughey and Harrelson executive produce alongside Natalie Sandy, David West Read, Trish Hofmann, Bill Bost, Jason Winer, David Finkel & Brett Baer and Jeremy Plager. Trent O’Donnell directs multiple episodes including the pilot.

articles.title: Star Wars Zero Company Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: Star Wars Zero Company from developers Bit Reactor and Respawn Entertainment takes a familiar genre, puts a beloved franchise in the thick of it and invites players to dive deep.
articles.body:
Star Wars Zero Company from developers Bit Reactor and Respawn Entertainment takes a familiar genre, puts a beloved franchise in the thick of it and invites players to dive deep.

Comparisons to genre heavyweights like XCOM are inescapable. No accident: Names who worked on XCOM and the criminally underrated Marvel's Midnight Suns have a hand in the efforts here.

The result is an easy to pick up and play experience with some surprising depth and a Star Wars tale that is very strong in narrative and memorable characters.
